justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a broadly stable outlook with only modest drift upward across time horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 223.5 was anchored primarily by recent price action and short-term momentum, assuming no major overnight catalysts. Markets tend to exhibit mean-reversion at very short horizons when no structural shock is imminent, so I kept the one-day estimate close to the prevailing level. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 224.0, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with long-run equity risk premium expectations. The one-month estimate of 225.0 follows the same logic extended further, incorporating a small but positive expected return while acknowledging that a single month is still a short enough window that the drift adds only marginally to the base level.

The confidence interval widths reflect how uncertainty compounds with time. At one day, the 90% interval of 218–229 is relatively tight because daily realized volatility in broad equity indices is historically constrained, and within a single session the range of plausible outcomes is bounded unless a specific catalyst is known. By one week, the interval widens to 212–236, capturing the possibility of macroeconomic data releases, central bank communications, or geopolitical developments that could shift sentiment meaningfully. At one month, the interval of 203–247 is substantially wider, acknowledging that over four to five weeks, a compounding of surprises, shifts in growth or inflation expectations, and evolving risk appetite can move prices considerably in either direction.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside the stated intervals. On the downside, a sharper-than-expected deterioration in economic data — such as a weak jobs report, a surprise contraction in manufacturing activity, or renewed stress in the banking or credit markets — could drive prices well below the lower bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon. A hawkish policy surprise from a major central bank, especially if it signals rates staying higher for longer than markets currently price, could similarly compress valuations rapidly. On the upside, a meaningful de-escalation of geopolitical tensions, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, or dovish forward guidance could produce a rally that breaches the upper bounds of my intervals.

It is also worth noting that the intervals I provided assume a roughly log-normal return distribution, which tends to underweight the probability of tail events. In practice, equity markets exhibit fat tails, meaning extreme outcomes — both crashes and melt-ups — occur more frequently than a Gaussian model implies. Black swan events, such as a sudden credit event, a major geopolitical shock, or an unexpected policy reversal, are by definition difficult to assign probabilities to but represent genuine sources of outcomes outside my stated ranges.
